question: Can task-loss model stitching provide a more operational comparison of neural representations than geometric similarity measures, and does it show that independently trained or more highly resourced vision models learn interchangeable internal features?

key_findings.claim: The paper defines a representation's stitching loss as the best downstream task loss obtainable after inserting a stitcher from a restricted family into a fixed upper network.
key_findings.evidence: Equation 1 takes the infimum of the task loss over stitchers between candidate representation r and the frozen layers above level l of model A; the reported penalty subtracts the original loss of A.

key_findings.claim: The operational quantity is deliberately asymmetric, task-specific, decoder-specific, and stitch-family-specific rather than a general metric between two representations.
key_findings.evidence: Sections 2-3 fix A's upper network and task loss, optimize only the adapter from r into A, and note explicitly that a representation can replace another in one direction but not vice versa.

key_findings.claim: The experiments train the adapter on task labels and estimate its penalty on held-out task examples while freezing both constituent models.
key_findings.evidence: The text says gradient optimization approximates Equation 1 on the training set and test loss estimates the penalty; CNN stitchers are a 1x1 convolution bracketed by BatchNorm layers and the Vision Transformer stitcher is token-wise linear.

key_findings.claim: Across the selected CIFAR-10 architectures, two models trained with different random seeds can be joined at the tested block boundaries with little classification-error increase.
key_findings.evidence: Figure 2A covers ResNet-18 at three widths, ResNet-164, Myrtle-CNN, and a CIFAR-5m-pretrained Vision Transformer; the text reports two initialized models per architecture and low loss for every independently optimized hybrid.

key_findings.claim: Supervised and selected self-supervised ImageNet ResNet-50 models are reported to be task-compatible after alignment despite substantially varying CKA values.
key_findings.evidence: Figure 2B compares a supervised target with SwAV, SimCLR, and DINO sources; Section 5 reports penalties no larger than about five percentage points while a CIFAR SimCLR comparison in the supplement is summarized as CKA 0.35-0.9 versus at most three percentage points of stitching penalty.

key_findings.claim: The one-way experiments support a limited decodability result: features learned with more samples, epochs, or width can often improve a weaker fixed classifier after supervised linear-convolutional alignment.
key_findings.evidence: Figure 2C and Figure 3 compare sources trained on 5K, 10K, or 25K images, at 40, 80, or 160 epochs, and at 0.25x, 1x, or 2x width; stronger-to-weaker substitutions tend to help and the reverse substitutions tend to hurt.

key_findings.claim: A freeze-training follow-up recovers most CIFAR-10 accuracy after selecting early and late layers suggested by the stitching profile.
key_findings.evidence: Section 6 says the first three and last three layers are trained with 5K samples, frozen, and the remaining layers trained with the full data, ending within two percentage points of the full-data network.

key_findings.claim: The formal interpretation of the penalty contains a sign error.
key_findings.evidence: The paper defines penalty as stitched loss minus base loss, then says a non-negative penalty means r is at least as good. For a loss, at-least-as-good requires a non-positive penalty; the plots themselves treat negative error differences as improvements.

key_findings.claim: Low task-loss penalty establishes sufficiency for one fixed decoder and task, not identity, geometric similarity, or general interchangeability of the source and target representations.
key_findings.evidence: Equation 1 ignores every source feature the fixed upper network does not use and evaluates only the information that the learned adapter can present to that decoder. The paper itself acknowledges task dependence and asymmetry, while later prose repeatedly promotes the result to nearly equivalent or essentially the same representations.

anchors.section: Section 3, Ignoring spurious features and Asymmetry

key_findings.claim: A task-loss-trained stitcher can manufacture target-useful, out-of-distribution activations rather than match the target representation distribution.
key_findings.evidence: The objective constrains only final task loss and contains no intermediate activation-matching or support constraint. Balogh and Jelasity's 2025 direct audit later demonstrates self-similarity and layer-order anomalies and attributes them to out-of-distribution target activations produced by task-loss matching.

key_findings.claim: The random-network control does not show that early-layer stitching and CKA are discriminative where many of the broad similarity claims are made.
key_findings.evidence: Section 2 says the random-source penalty is especially high only for high l, and Figure 2A shows the random curve near the trained curves at early interfaces. Thus an untrained source is compatible under the proposed test over part of the depth range.

key_findings.claim: The claim that BatchNorm does not change stitcher representation capacity is unsupported and conflates output dimension with hypothesis class.
key_findings.evidence: The actual CNN adapter includes BatchNorm before and after the 1x1 convolution. Learned affine normalization, sample-dependent training behavior, and running statistics change the function, invariances, conditioning, and data dependence relative to a bare convolution even if the channel dimension is unchanged.

key_findings.claim: A negative penalty does not by itself prove that the incoming representation is intrinsically better because it includes a newly supervised optimization stage absent from the base model comparison.
key_findings.evidence: The adapter is trained on task labels after both endpoints have been trained; gains can therefore arise from reoptimization, regularization, normalization, or a favorable projection into the fixed decoder, not solely from the quality of r.

key_findings.claim: The paper's population-level language about almost all SGD minima is much broader than its sampling design supports.
key_findings.evidence: The central conjecture concerns natural architectures and distributions and says independently trained networks will almost certainly be connected, but Figure 2A uses two random initializations per architecture on one principal dataset and supplies no confidence intervals, seed distribution, failure-rate estimate, or formal sampling test.

key_findings.claim: Stitching connectivity is not a continuous low-loss path and does not establish a coherent transformation between two parameter settings.
key_findings.evidence: Each hybrid S_i uses a separately optimized stitcher, with no constraint relating adjacent adapters; the paper explicitly concedes that the finite sequence does not technically define a parameter-space path.

key_findings.claim: Same-distribution accuracy can hide incompatible cues, invariances, adversarial behavior, calibration, and out-of-distribution generalization.
key_findings.evidence: Every focal metric is ordinary classification loss on CIFAR-10 or ImageNet. No intervention holds final accuracy fixed while changing relied-on cues, and no robust, transfer, corruption, calibration, metamer, or OOD evaluation is reported.

key_findings.claim: The disagreement with CKA is not evidence that one method is universally more faithful because the two quantities answer different questions.
key_findings.evidence: CKA is a symmetric task-independent comparison of activation geometry, whereas the focal score is a directed, task-trained sufficiency test through one decoder. A low stitch penalty and modest CKA can both be correct without contradiction.

key_findings.claim: The 'more is better' study cannot isolate representational quality without a fully specified and matched adapter-label budget.
key_findings.evidence: Section 6 varies the data used to train source representations, but the main paper does not state, for each comparison, which examples and labels train the stitcher. Seeing more labels than the weaker top would directly confound the result; seeing the same labels still introduces a new supervised optimization absent from the endpoint.

key_findings.claim: The freeze-training demonstration is exploratory rather than an independent validation of the layer-quality interpretation.
key_findings.evidence: Layers are selected from stitching behavior and then assessed on the same dataset family, without an independent selection split, random-layer control, uncertainty, wall-clock measurement, or comparison to compute-matched freezing schedules.

key_findings.claim: The paper and supplement leave important reproduction and uncertainty details unresolved.
key_findings.evidence: They give optimizer families and many base-model hyperparameters but not a complete per-interface stitcher schedule, stopping and model-selection rule, batch size, seed count for every curve, uncertainty, or raw results. The supplement's Object/Animal list names only nine CIFAR-10 classes, calls random replacement at rate one '100% label noise' although about one tenth remain correct in expectation, and contains an unresolved timm citation marker.

key_findings.claim: The study's strongest defensible conclusion is narrower than 'all roads lead to Rome': selected vision representations often contain information that a small supervised adapter can make useful to a selected frozen classifier.
key_findings.evidence: That interpretation follows directly from Equation 1 and the reported test-error curves while avoiding unsupported claims about full representational identity, shared causal features, or universal SGD minima.

method.core_idea: Compare a candidate intermediate representation with the bottom of a target model by learning a low-capacity adapter into the target's frozen upper layers and expressing compatibility in downstream task-loss units.
method.mechanism: For each source-target interface, train a 1x1-convolution-plus-BatchNorm adapter for CNNs or a token-wise linear adapter for a Vision Transformer on task data, evaluate the resulting hybrid on held-out examples, and subtract the target model's original loss. Sweep depth and direction across independently seeded, self-supervised, label-perturbed, data-scaled, time-scaled, and width-scaled models.
assumptions: A low-capacity task-trained adapter cannot learn enough task structure to obscure meaningful differences between its inputs.
Information useful to one fixed upper network is an adequate proxy for the quality of the whole representation.
The chosen adapter family captures harmless coordinate changes but not substantive representational changes.
BatchNorm around a 1x1 convolution changes optimization but not the relevant adapter capacity.
Ordinary in-distribution classification error captures the functional properties relevant to representation equivalence.
Training the adapter with labels does not confound comparisons among source representations trained with different label or sample budgets.
Two seeds per architecture are sufficient evidence for statements about typical or almost all SGD minima.
Separately optimized hybrids across layer depth form a meaningful notion of connectivity despite not constituting one continuous path.
CIFAR-10 and ImageNet vision results transfer to broader claims about neural representations.
Negative stitching penalty is attributable to a better source representation rather than adapter reoptimization or normalization effects.

techniques.role: Optimizes a small bridge between a source representation and a frozen target decoder using downstream loss.
Measures one-way replacement cost in interpretable task-loss units relative to the target model.
Uses BatchNorm, a 1x1 convolution, and BatchNorm to map between convolutional feature tensors.
Uses a token-wise linear transformation between selected Vision Transformer blocks.
Repeats independently optimized substitutions across block boundaries to form a layerwise compatibility profile.
Stitches an untrained random bottom network to test whether the adapter trivially rescues every source.
Contrasts task-grounded compatibility with a symmetric activation-geometry measure.
Varies source sample count, training epochs, and width to test directed decodability into weaker models.
Changes coarse-label and random-label distributions while holding the image distribution fixed.
Uses the observed depth profile to motivate a reduced-data freeze-training schedule.

evaluations.setting: CIFAR-10 models of several convolutional architectures plus a CIFAR-5m-pretrained Vision Transformer, with two independently initialized models per architecture
evaluations.metric: Test-error difference after stitching at selected depths
evaluations.result: Figure 2A reports penalties generally within about three percentage points for trained pairs, whereas a random bottom becomes markedly worse at deeper interfaces.
evaluations.baseline: The controls are the unstitched endpoints and one random-bottom condition; there are no error bars, distribution over many seed pairs, or direct-activation matching baseline.

evaluations.setting: ImageNet ResNet-50 models trained end-to-end or with SwAV, SimCLR, and DINO self-supervision
evaluations.metric: Top-1 error penalty across block depth
evaluations.result: Figure 2B reports broad stitchability within roughly five percentage points despite SimCLR's lower 68.8% base accuracy and the other models' approximately 75% plus or minus one point.
evaluations.baseline: The comparison lacks activation-support checks, robust/OOD outcomes, repeated adapter seeds, and uncertainty.

evaluations.setting: CIFAR-10 SimCLR versus supervised ResNet-18 in both stitch directions
evaluations.metric: Task-error penalty and linear CKA by depth
evaluations.result: The main text summarizes supplemental curves as at most about three percentage points of stitching penalty while CKA ranges approximately 0.35-0.9.
evaluations.baseline: The two values measure directed task sufficiency and symmetric geometry respectively, so their disagreement is not a head-to-head accuracy contest.

evaluations.setting: CIFAR-10 sources trained with 5K, 10K, or 25K samples and inserted into a 10K-sample target
evaluations.result: The 25K source improves the weaker target at deeper interfaces, while the 5K source degrades more rapidly in middle and late layers.
evaluations.baseline: The adapter's exact labeled-example budget and the effect of its new supervised optimization are not isolated.

evaluations.setting: CIFAR-10 ResNet-18 checkpoints at 40, 80, and 160 epochs
evaluations.metric: Directed test-error penalty into the 80-epoch checkpoint
evaluations.result: Longer-trained features tend to improve the 80-epoch decoder, shorter-trained features degrade it, and early layers appear to converge sooner.
evaluations.baseline: Checkpoint provenance and independence are not analyzed, and no independently trained same-budget control separates trajectory proximity from representational convergence.

evaluations.metric: Directional test-error penalty and supplemental CKA
evaluations.result: Wider-to-narrower substitutions can improve accuracy while narrower-to-wider substitutions tend to hurt; the 0.25x-to-2x CKA range is summarized as about 0.7-0.9.
evaluations.baseline: A learned projection from a higher-dimensional source can expose extra decodable features without establishing that the two representations are the same type.

evaluations.setting: CIFAR-10 binary coarse labels and random replacement of 10%, 50%, or 100% of labels
evaluations.metric: Stitching penalty into a standard ten-class target by depth
evaluations.result: Early layers remain relatively compatible under weaker labels, with larger deep penalties and a stronger failure for full-rate random replacement.
evaluations.baseline: The supplemental coarse-label list omits Bird, and full-rate random replacement retains the original class about ten percent of the time in expectation.

evaluations.setting: Freeze-training schedule motivated by the 5K-versus-full-data layer profile
evaluations.metric: Final CIFAR-10 accuracy relative to ordinary full-data training
evaluations.result: Training the first three and last three layers on 5K samples, freezing them, then training the remainder on all samples ends within two percentage points of the reference network.
evaluations.baseline: No random-layer, compute-matched schedule, independent selection set, wall-clock, or uncertainty comparison is reported.

evaluations.setting: Supplemental ablation of convolutional stitcher kernel size
evaluations.metric: CIFAR-10 test error at several stitch locations
evaluations.result: The authors describe kernel size as having minimal impact, although the displayed layer-6 error changes visibly from roughly 0.10 to 0.122 in a single curve.
evaluations.baseline: There are no repeated runs, uncertainty intervals, parameter-matched controls, or distribution-matching objectives.

limitations: Task-loss stitching measures one-way sufficiency for a selected decoder, task, adapter class, optimizer, and adapter-training dataset rather than general representation identity.
The penalty definition is followed by an incorrect sign interpretation.
A task-only adapter objective permits out-of-distribution target activations and layer-similarity anomalies.
The random-source control is weak at early interfaces, where an untrained source can also be stitched successfully.
BatchNorm before and after the convolution adds learned, stateful, data-dependent behavior whose capacity is not audited.
Negative penalty is confounded by a newly trained supervised adapter and cannot be assigned solely to source-representation quality.
Two endpoint seeds per architecture do not support claims about almost all SGD minima.
The discrete hybrids use unrelated independently optimized adapters and do not form a continuous connectivity path.
Ordinary in-distribution accuracy cannot reveal whether models use different cues, invariances, robustness mechanisms, or OOD behavior.
The more-data experiment does not clearly isolate the stitcher's labeled-data budget.
Self-supervised-to-supervised compatibility shows decodability for a supervised target task, not identical pretraining representations.
The freeze-training study reuses the same dataset family for layer selection and evaluation and omits compute-matched controls.
Stitcher batch size, complete schedules, stopping, model selection, per-curve seeds, uncertainty, and raw result tables are not fully reported.
Supplemental label definitions and the phrase 100% label noise are operationally ambiguous.
All focal evidence is from image classification; there is no language, structured prediction, generation, transfer, calibration, or deployment study.
No official implementation, raw results, or reproducible experiment artifact was found for the focal paper.
failure_modes: A stitcher can map source activations outside the target representation support while preserving or improving final accuracy.
Two models can use different causal or spurious cues yet appear compatible on the same IID test set.
Early random features can remain decodable enough to produce deceptively low penalties.
An overpowered or data-dependent adapter can learn task structure rather than a harmless change of coordinates.
An underpowered adapter can falsely declare equivalent representations incompatible because its invariance family is misspecified.
One direction can look compatible while the reverse direction fails, so symmetric language obscures information loss.
Changing the adapter-label budget can reverse a more-data conclusion independently of source quality.
Layerwise adapters can each solve a separate alignment problem while providing no coherent path or shared basis across depth.
Final accuracy can remain stable while robustness, calibration, subgroup behavior, or transfer collapses.
BatchNorm running statistics can leak dataset-specific support and make deployment behavior differ from the measured test protocol.
Selecting freeze points from the same compatibility curves can overfit the reported schedule.
A small number of successful seed pairs can conceal a substantial tail of non-stitchable minima.
reusable_insights: Treat model stitching as a conditional decoder-sufficiency test and name the target task, decoder, adapter family, direction, data budget, and optimizer in every claim.
Report a matrix of directions and tasks rather than collapsing compatibility into one scalar.
Combine task loss with direct activation matching, target-support distance, and cycle or metamer consistency so successful adapters cannot rely on OOD activations.
Use random, label-permuted, cue-swapped, and capacity-swept adapters as calibrated negative controls at every depth.
Separate adapter data from endpoint training data and match labeled examples, optimization steps, and hyperparameter search across comparisons.
Evaluate causal cue reliance, robustness, calibration, transfer, and OOD behavior alongside IID accuracy.
Estimate seed-pair distributions with confidence intervals before making claims about typical SGD minima.
Distinguish a finite family of independently solved hybrids from a continuous path and test whether adapters compose coherently across adjacent layers.
Use stitch profiles to generate hypotheses about freeze schedules, then validate them on independent datasets with random-layer and compute-matched controls.
Preserve the method's most useful feature: task-loss units give an interpretable operational cost when the scope of that interpretation is stated narrowly.

For heterogeneous foundation models, compare intermediate matching, final-feature matching, and task loss rather than assuming one stitching objective transfers across architecture and pretraining regimes.
Make the equivalence relation explicit: decodable information, activation geometry, invariance structure, causal features, and deployable interchangeability are different targets.
open_questions: Which adapter families are expressive enough to correct coordinate mismatch but too weak to learn new task structure?
Can target-support constraints prevent task-loss matching from creating out-of-distribution intermediate activations without discarding useful functional alignment?
When do forward compatibility, backward compatibility, direct matching, and cycle consistency agree?
How many seed pairs and architectures are needed to estimate the prevalence rather than merely the existence of stitching connectivity?
Do independently optimized layerwise adapters admit a shared low-dimensional alignment or compositional law across depth?
Does compatibility survive cue-conflict, adversarial, corruption, subgroup, calibration, and distribution-shift tests?
How should adapter training labels be budgeted when source models were trained with different amounts of supervision?
Can one preregister a null distribution for random or label-destroyed sources at each layer and architecture?
Which aspects of self-supervised representations remain incompatible after controlling for the supervised target head and adapter?
Does a negative penalty persist when the base target receives an equally budgeted reoptimization or calibration stage?
Can freeze schedules derived on one dataset or seed transfer to a new dataset, architecture, and compute regime?
What is the right stitching protocol for language models, sequence generation, multimodal foundation models, and architectures with unequal tokenization or spatial resolution?

competitive_landscape.title: Understanding Image Representations by Measuring Their Equivariance and Equivalence
competitive_landscape.difference: Lenc and Vedaldi introduced learned mappings between intermediate vision representations and evaluated equivariance and equivalence six years earlier. The focal work extends this into directed task-loss penalties, depth sweeps, resource comparisons, and a connectivity conjecture.

competitive_landscape.title: SVCCA: Singular Vector Canonical Correlation Analysis for Deep Learning Dynamics and Interpretability
competitive_landscape.difference: SVCCA compares activation subspaces and training dynamics without fitting a downstream task adapter. It targets shared geometry rather than the focal method's directed decodability, so the two methods expose different equivalence notions.

competitive_landscape.title: Insights on Representational Similarity in Neural Networks with Canonical Correlation
competitive_landscape.difference: PWCCA weights canonical directions by their contribution to the original representation. It offers a task-independent structural profile but cannot express the one-way better-than relation that motivates the focal score.

competitive_landscape.title: Towards Understanding Learning Representations: To What Extent Do Different Neural Networks Learn the Same Representation
competitive_landscape.difference: Wang et al. search for shared and exclusive subspaces across independently trained networks and often find only partial overlap. The focal work instead asks whether a learned task adapter lets one frozen decoder consume the other representation.

competitive_landscape.title: Similarity of Neural Network Representations Revisited
competitive_landscape.difference: Kornblith et al. derive CKA's invariances and use it to compare activation geometry across width and depth. The focal paper gains directional, task-unit interpretation by fitting adapters but necessarily loses task independence and metric symmetry.

competitive_landscape.title: Do Wide and Deep Networks Learn the Same Things? Uncovering How Neural Network Representations Vary with Width and Depth
competitive_landscape.difference: Nguyen, Raghu, and Kornblith use CKA across width, depth, seed, and training to identify block structure and specialization. The focal work interprets some CKA differences as task-irrelevant because a learned adapter preserves classification loss.

competitive_landscape.title: Similarity and Matching of Neural Network Representations
competitive_landscape.difference: Csiszarik et al. independently develop representation matching and stitching, systematically comparing matching losses and sparse transformations. The focal paper emphasizes empirical narratives about SGD connectivity and more resources rather than the matching problem itself.

competitive_landscape.title: Grounding Representation Similarity Through Statistical Testing
competitive_landscape.difference: Ding, Denain, and Steinhardt evaluate similarity measures through explicit statistical tests tied to downstream properties. Their framework makes the grounding claim falsifiable without equating task-adapter success with full representation similarity.

competitive_landscape.title: Generalized Shape Metrics on Neural Representations
competitive_landscape.difference: Williams et al. place common representation comparisons in a metric-space framework with explicit transformation groups. The focal score is intentionally nonmetric and decoder-conditioned, making its invariance class operational but harder to compare universally.

competitive_landscape.title: Git Re-Basin: Merging Models modulo Permutation Symmetries
competitive_landscape.difference: Git Re-Basin explicitly aligns permutation symmetries and merges independently trained models into low-barrier parameter paths. It addresses connectivity in a coherent parameter basis, whereas the focal stitching sequence uses a different trained adapter at each discrete depth.

competitive_landscape.title: Model Stitching: Looking For Functional Similarity Between Representations
competitive_landscape.difference: This follow-up finds unexpectedly successful stitching between noncorresponding and distant layers, illustrating that task performance can remain high even when architectural position argues against a strong similarity interpretation.

competitive_landscape.title: On the Functional Similarity of Robust and Non-Robust Neural Representations
competitive_landscape.difference: Balogh and Jelasity show that robust and nonrobust features can remain compatible for ordinary accuracy while robust accuracy behaves very differently. This directly demonstrates that one focal task loss can conceal another essential functional property.

competitive_landscape.title: Stitchable Neural Networks
competitive_landscape.difference: Pan et al. jointly train a network family so blocks can be stitched into many accuracy-efficiency configurations. This converts compatibility from a post-hoc diagnostic into a design objective, but it no longer tests independently emerged representations.

competitive_landscape.title: What Representations Do Deep Neural Networks Learn? A Perspective from Decodable Information
competitive_landscape.difference: Harvey et al. argue that probe results should be interpreted as information decodability under a declared readout rather than direct representation content. That vocabulary precisely narrows what the focal frozen-decoder-plus-adapter test establishes.

competitive_landscape.title: The Platonic Representation Hypothesis
competitive_landscape.difference: Huh et al. assemble cross-model and cross-modality evidence for convergence toward a shared statistical model of reality. Their much broader hypothesis amplifies the need to separate geometric alignment, task decodability, and shared causal structure highlighted by the focal audit.

competitive_landscape.title: How Not to Stitch Representations to Measure Similarity: Task Loss Matching Versus Direct Matching
competitive_landscape.difference: Balogh and Jelasity reproduce task-loss matching anomalies in which distant layers appear more similar than corresponding layers and a layer can appear less similar to itself than another layer. They trace the issue to OOD target activations and find direct matching avoids these failures.

competitive_landscape.title: On the Dataset Dependence of Representation Similarity
competitive_landscape.difference: Ciernik et al. show that representation-comparison conclusions depend on the sample distribution used to calculate them. The same concern applies doubly to stitching because both adapter fitting and penalty evaluation introduce dataset choices.

competitive_landscape.title: Grounding Functional Similarity by Invariance-Aware Model Stitching
competitive_landscape.difference: Athanasiadis, Karmush, and Felsberg show that standard forward stitching can rate models as similar even when they rely on different cues. Their backward-compatibility and metamer constraints expose invariance differences that the focal IID task-loss test cannot see.

competitive_landscape.title: Revisiting Model Stitching In the Foundation Model Era
competitive_landscape.difference: Mai et al. find that ordinary intermediate matching and task-loss training struggle for shallow heterogeneous vision foundation-model stitches, while matching the target's penultimate features works better. Their systematic objective and task sweep limits the focal protocol's assumed portability.

novelty_assessment: Reviewer inference: the paper's meaningful 2021 contribution is not the original stitching mechanism, which dates to Lenc and Vedaldi, but its clear directed task-loss formulation, breadth of same-architecture vision sweeps, empirical 'more resources' substitutions, and the discrete stitching-connectivity conjecture. Those experiments established a useful operational diagnostic and inspired a substantial follow-up literature. The headline interpretation is nevertheless too broad. Equation 1 tests whether a newly trained, supervised, low-capacity map can expose source information to one frozen target decoder on one task. It does not establish representational identity, a shared causal basis, or a population theorem about SGD minima. The paper's sign error, two-seed design, stateful BatchNorm adapter, unspecified adapter-label budget in key comparisons, and lack of uncertainty constrain even the original empirical scope. Direct 2023-2026 work now shows that ordinary accuracy compatibility can coexist with different robustness, OOD activation support, cue reliance, invariances, and heterogeneous-model failures. A stronger successor would preregister direction, tasks, adapter capacity and data; combine task loss with direct matching, support and cycle tests; estimate seed distributions; and reserve 'similar representation' for claims that survive cue, robustness, transfer, and OOD falsifiers.
reviewer_notes: Read and visually inspected every page of the exact 12-page NeurIPS 2021 proceedings PDF at original render resolution, including all equations, three main figures, Table 1, captions, footnotes, acknowledgements, and references. Also obtained and inspected all five pages of the official NeurIPS supplemental PDF (https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper_files/paper/2021/file/01ded4259d101feb739b06c399e9cd9c-Supplemental.pdf; SHA-256 0ac7130252b62a9dbfb3ddc8b3057cc765e88e0fd32ba6217009ae2cf3f5d920), covering base-model settings, kernel and CKA ablations, fine-tuning, freeze training, and label definitions. Canonical anchors refer to the indexed main PDF; supplemental-only audit details are identified as such in evidence. Re-derived the penalty sign and conditional-sufficiency interpretation. Competitive research was refreshed through 2026-08-23 from primary CVF, NeurIPS, PMLR, AAAI, arXiv, and OpenReview records. Exact-title, author, venue, and code searches found the official supplement but no focal-paper implementation, raw results, or experiment artifact.
